title: The plural in every case: markets and quantities
objectives: I can put nouns into the plural in every case, and choose the nominative or the genitive form for the accusative plural.
I can form the genitive plural, including the forms with no ending and an inserted 'о' or 'е', such as 'пля́шок' and 'сесте́р'.
I can put adjectives, possessive pronouns and 'цей' and 'той' into the plural in every case.
I can use numbers, 'бага́то', 'ма́ло', 'кі́лька', 'до́сить' and words for weights and containers with the right form of the noun.
I can buy fruit and vegetables at a market, asking for amounts and prices.

vocabulary.note: Used for a man or a woman alike, and grammatically feminine whoever it names, so adjectives with it are feminine. The plural is 'лю́ди', on another stem; after 'дві', 'три' and 'чоти́ри' the form is 'люди́ни'.
The plural of 'люди́на'. Genitive and accusative 'люде́й', dative 'лю́дям', instrumental 'людьми́', locative 'на лю́дях'.

example.source: These people work at the market.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'кілогра́ма', as for other units of measure. 'Два кілогра́ми', 'п’ять кілогра́мів'. What is weighed follows in the genitive.

example.source: I'll take two kilograms of potatoes.

vocabulary.note: Genitive plural 'пля́шок', with an inserted 'о'. The contents follow in the genitive: 'пля́шка води́'.

example.source: There are three bottles of juice on the table.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'паке́та'. A paper or plastic bag, and the carton that milk and juice are sold in: 'паке́т молока́'.

example.target: Я купи́в паке́т молока́ й хліб.
example.source: I bought a carton of milk and some bread.
example.source_literal: I bought carton of-milk and bread.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'шматка́': the 'о' drops when an ending is added. Plural 'шматки́', genitive plural 'шматкі́в'.

example.source: Could I have a piece of cheese?

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'деся́тка'. A noun, not a numeral: eggs are sold by the ten, and the noun after it is in the genitive plural, 'деся́ток я́єць'.
With a verb it says how much: 'Він бага́то працю́є.' With a noun it names a quantity, and the noun goes in the genitive: plural for things you count, singular for things you do not.

example.source: Taras has a lot of friends.

vocabulary.note: The opposite of 'бага́то', used the same way, with a verb or with a noun in the genitive.

example.source: I don't have much time today.

vocabulary.note: A numeral of indefinite quantity: it counts things but names no exact number. It goes only with things you count, and the noun is in the genitive plural: 'кі́лька я́блук'.
With a noun in the genitive: 'до́сить хлі́ба'. Before an adjective or an adverb it means 'quite': 'до́сить до́бре', quite well.

example.source: A kilogram of tomatoes costs fifty hryvnias.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'о́гірка'. In the plural the stress moves to the ending: 'огірки́', 'огіркі́в', 'з огірка́ми'.

example.target: Я купи́ла кілогра́м слив для бабу́сі.
example.source: I bought a kilogram of plums for Grandma.
example.source_literal: I bought kilogram of-plums for grandmother.

vocabulary.note: Genitive plural 'ви́шень', with an inserted 'е'. The same word names the tree.

example.target: У ли́пні на ри́нку бага́то ви́шень.
example.source: In July there are a lot of sour cherries at the market.
example.source_literal: In July on market many of-sour-cherries.

vocabulary.note: Genitive plural 'полуни́ць': the 'ц' stays soft at the end of the word, so it is written with 'ь'.

example.source: Half a kilogram of strawberries, please.

dialogues.title: At the market with a list
dialogues.context: On Saturday morning Sam and Oksana shop at the market near Oksana's home with a list from her mother. They say 'ти' to each other and 'ви' to Bohdan, who sells fruit and vegetables.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, що нам тре́ба купи́ти?
lines.source: Sam, what do we need to buy?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what to-us necessary to-buy?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Кілогра́м помідо́рів, два кілогра́ми карто́плі, кі́лька огіркі́в і деся́ток я́єць.
lines.source: A kilogram of tomatoes, two kilograms of potatoes, a few cucumbers and ten eggs.
lines.source_literal: Kilogram of-tomatoes, two kilograms of-potatoes, several of-cucumbers and ten of-eggs.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І полуни́ці. Ма́ма ду́же лю́бить полуни́ці.
lines.source: And strawberries. Mom loves strawberries.
lines.source_literal: And strawberries. Mom very loves strawberries.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день! Що вам да́ти?
lines.source: Hello! What can I get you?
lines.source_literal: Good day! What to-you to-give?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Да́йте, будь ла́ска, кілогра́м помідо́рів. Скі́льки вони́ ко́штують?
lines.source: A kilogram of tomatoes, please. How much are they?
lines.source_literal: Give, be kindness, kilogram of-tomatoes. How-much they cost?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Кілогра́м ко́штує со́рок гри́вень.
lines.source: Forty hryvnias a kilogram.
lines.source_literal: Kilogram costs forty of-hryvnias.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре. І два кілогра́ми карто́плі, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Fine. And two kilograms of potatoes, please.
lines.source_literal: Well. And two kilograms of-potatoes, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Ось. Огірки́ теж? Вони́ сього́дні ду́же смачні́.
lines.source: Here you are. Cucumbers too? They're very good today.
lines.source_literal: Here. Cucumbers too? They today very tasty.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, п’ять огіркі́в. А я́йця у вас є?
lines.source: Yes, five cucumbers. And do you have eggs?
lines.source_literal: Yes, five of-cucumbers. And eggs at you are?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Є. Деся́ток? Два деся́тки?
lines.source: Yes. Ten? Twenty?
lines.source_literal: There-are. Ten? Two tens?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Оди́н деся́ток. А полуни́ці у вас є?
lines.source: Ten. And do you have strawberries?
lines.source_literal: One ten. And strawberries at you are?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: На жаль, полуни́ць сього́дні нема́є. Є сли́ви й ви́шні.
lines.source: Unfortunately, there are no strawberries today. There are plums and sour cherries.
lines.source_literal: On regret, of-strawberries today there-is-not. There-are plums and sour-cherries.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Да́йте нам півкілогра́ма ви́шень. Скі́льки ра́зом?
lines.source: Give us half a kilogram of sour cherries. How much is that altogether?
lines.source_literal: Give to-us half-of-kilogram of-sour-cherries. How-much together?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Ра́зом сто п’ятдеся́т гри́вень. Дя́кую!
lines.source: A hundred and fifty hryvnias altogether. Thank you!
lines.source_literal: Together hundred fifty of-hryvnias. I-thank!

dialogues.title: Ten people for dinner
dialogues.context: Olena is having a family dinner at her apartment on Sunday. She phones her brother Taras, and they count the guests and the food. They say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, скі́льки люде́й бу́де в неді́лю?
lines.source: Taras, how many people will there be on Sunday?
lines.source_literal: Taras, how-many of-people will-be on Sunday?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ма́ма й та́то, бабу́ся, дя́дько з ті́ткою і ї́хні ді́ти.
lines.source: Mom and Dad, Grandma, our uncle and aunt and their children.
lines.source_literal: Mom and dad, grandmother, uncle with aunt and their children.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Скі́льки в них діте́й?
lines.source: How many children do they have?
lines.source_literal: How-many at them of-children?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Три дити́ни. А ще ти і я.
lines.source: Three. And then there's you and me.
lines.source_literal: Three children. And more you and I.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Це де́сять люде́й. Бага́то!
lines.source: That's ten people. That's a lot!
lines.source_literal: This ten of-people. Many!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Що ти бу́деш ва́рити?
lines.source: What are you going to cook?
lines.source_literal: What you will-be to-cook?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Борщ і варе́ники. Мені́ тре́ба три кілогра́ми карто́плі й п’ять бурякі́в.
lines.source: Borscht and varenyky. I need three kilograms of potatoes and five beets.
lines.source_literal: Borscht and varenyky. To-me necessary three kilograms of-potatoes and five of-beets.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А для діте́й? Їм подо́баються полуни́ці.
lines.source: And for the children? They like strawberries.
lines.source_literal: And for children? To-them please strawberries.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До́бре, я куплю́ два кілогра́ми полуни́ць. І шість пля́шок со́ку.
lines.source: OK, I'll buy two kilograms of strawberries. And six bottles of juice.
lines.source_literal: Well, I will-buy two kilograms of-strawberries. And six of-bottles of-juice.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А я куплю́ хліб і вели́кий шмато́к си́ру.
lines.source: And I'll buy bread and a big piece of cheese.
lines.source_literal: And I will-buy bread and big piece of-cheese.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Дя́кую! І ще деся́ток я́єць для варе́ників, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Thanks! And ten eggs for the varenyky too, please.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! And more ten of-eggs for varenyky, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Звича́йно. А в те́бе до́сить скля́нок?
lines.source: Of course. And do you have enough glasses?
lines.source_literal: Of course. And at you enough of-glasses?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, у ме́не ма́ло скля́нок.
lines.source: No, I don't have many glasses.
lines.source_literal: No, at me few of-glasses.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я дам тобі́ свої́. До неді́лі!
lines.source: I'll give you mine. See you on Sunday!
lines.source_literal: I will-give to-you own. Until Sunday!

dialogues.title: Sam's first market
dialogues.context: On Monday Sam's teacher Iryna Petrivna asks him about his weekend. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, що ви роби́ли на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Sam, what did you do at the weekend?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what you did on weekend?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У субо́ту я був на ри́нку з Окса́ною. Там було́ ду́же бага́то люде́й!
lines.source: On Saturday I was at the market with Oksana. There were so many people there!
lines.source_literal: On Saturday I was on market with Oksana. There was very many of-people!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У субо́ту на ри́нках завжди́ бага́то люде́й. Що ви купи́ли?
lines.source: There are always a lot of people at the markets on Saturday. What did you buy?
lines.source_literal: On Saturday on markets always many of-people. What you bought?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Помідо́ри, огірки́, карто́плю, я́йця й півкілогра́ма ви́шень.
lines.source: Tomatoes, cucumbers, potatoes, eggs and half a kilogram of sour cherries.
lines.source_literal: Tomatoes, cucumbers, potatoes, eggs and half-of-kilogram of-sour-cherries.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А з продавця́ми ви говори́ли украї́нською?
lines.source: And did you speak Ukrainian with the sellers?
lines.source_literal: And with sellers you spoke by-Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так! Продавці́ мене́ розумі́ли, а я їх розумі́в не завжди́.
lines.source: Yes! The sellers understood me, but I didn't always understand them.
lines.source_literal: Yes! Sellers me understood, and I them understood not always.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Чому́?
lines.source: Why?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Вони́ гово́рять ду́же шви́дко, а чи́сла я ще розумі́ю пові́льно.
lines.source: They speak very fast, and I'm still slow with numbers.
lines.source_literal: They speak very quickly, and numbers I still understand slowly.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Розумі́ю. А кому́ ви купи́ли ви́шні?
lines.source: I see. And who did you buy the sour cherries for?
lines.source_literal: I-understand. And to-whom you bought sour-cherries?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мої́м сусі́дам. Вони́ ду́же лю́блять ви́шні.
lines.source: For my neighbors. They love sour cherries.
lines.source_literal: To-my to-neighbors. They very love sour-cherries.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре, Се́ме. Купу́йте на ри́нку ча́сто й говорі́ть із людьми́!
lines.source: Very good, Sam. Shop at the market often and talk to people!
lines.source_literal: Very well, Sam. Buy on market often and speak with people!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Обов’язко́во! У субо́ту я теж бу́ду на ри́нку.
lines.source: Definitely! I'll be at the market on Saturday too.
lines.source_literal: Without-fail! On Saturday I too will-be on market.

grammar.title: The plural in every case
grammar.explanation:
You already know the nominative plural: '-и' after a hard stem ('помідо́ри', 'кни́ги'), '-і' after a soft stem and after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ' ('вчителі́', 'гру́ші'), and '-а' or '-я' for neuter nouns ('я́блука', 'міста́'). The plural has its own form for every other case too, and in one way it is simpler than the singular: the dative, the instrumental and the locative have the same endings for all three genders.

Each of these three shared endings has a hard form and a soft form:

- dative, answering 'кому́?' or 'чому́?': '-ам' or '-ям', as in 'помідо́рам', 'ді́тям'
- instrumental, answering 'ким?' or 'чим?': '-ами' or '-ями', as in 'пля́шками', 'дру́зями'
- locative, answering 'на кому́?' or 'на чому́?': '-ах' or '-ях', as in 'на ри́нках', 'у міста́х'

The soft forms, with 'я', follow a soft consonant, a vowel or 'й': 'дру́зі', 'дру́зям'; 'музе́ї', 'у музе́ях'; 'неді́лі', 'неді́лям'. The consonants 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' and 'щ' cannot be soft, so the hard forms follow them, even though their nominative plural ends in '-і': 'гру́ші', 'гру́шам'; 'ключі́', 'ключа́ми'; 'пло́щі', 'на пло́щах'.

The dative, the instrumental and the locative usually keep the stress of the nominative plural: 'се́стри', 'се́страм'; 'ві́кна', 'ві́кнами'; 'міста́', 'у міста́х'.

Three forms remain. The genitive plural is the one plural case whose ending depends on gender, and the next note explains it. The accusative plural has no ending of its own: it is the nominative form or the genitive form, as the note on adjectives explains. The vocative plural is the same as the nominative: 'Дру́зі, приві́т!'

The phrase 'на вихідни́х', at the weekend, which you learned whole, is a locative plural. 'Вихідні́' declines like an adjective, and '-их' is the adjective ending of the locative plural.

The table declines three model nouns in the plural, one of each gender.

examples.source: I'm phoning my brothers.
I gave the children apples.

examples.target: Ми ї́демо на мо́ре з дру́зями.
examples.source: We are going to the sea with friends.
There are a lot of shops in the cities.
Hi, friends!

grammar.title: The genitive plural: endings and no ending
grammar.explanation:
The genitive plural answers 'кого́?' or 'чого́?'. It is the plural form you will need most: after 'п’ять' and higher numbers, after words of quantity such as 'бага́то', after 'нема́є', and after prepositions that take the genitive, such as 'для', 'без' and 'бі́ля'. Its ending depends on the gender and on the last sound of the stem.

Masculine nouns take '-ів', written '-їв' after a vowel or 'й', because 'й' plus 'і' is written 'ї':

- 'помідо́р', 'помідо́рів'
- 'вчи́тель', 'вчителі́в'
- 'ключ', 'ключі́в'
- 'музе́й', 'музе́їв'

Feminine nouns in '-а' or '-я', neuter nouns in '-о' and a few neuter nouns in '-е', such as 'яйце́', take no ending at all. The genitive plural is the bare stem: the noun loses its final vowel and adds nothing. 'Кни́га' becomes 'книг', 'гру́ша' becomes 'груш', 'сли́ва' becomes 'слив', 'я́блуко' becomes 'я́блук' and 'мі́сто' becomes 'міст'. English has no form like this, so learn it as the form that shows the case by having no ending.

A bare stem cannot always end a word as it stands. When it would end in two consonants that Ukrainian does not put together at the end of a word, an 'о' or an 'е' appears between them:

- 'пля́шка', 'пля́шок'
- 'ви́шня', 'ви́шень'
- 'сестра́', 'сесте́р'
- 'вікно́', 'ві́кон'
- 'яйце́', 'я́єць'

This is the same kind of vowel as the 'о' of 'ри́нок' and the 'е' of 'сі́чень', which drop out when an ending is added ('на ри́нку', 'сі́чня'). There a vowel disappears when the syllable opens; here a vowel appears when the word is left without an ending. The usual choice is 'о' before 'к' ('пля́шок', 'ча́шок', 'ру́чок'), and 'е' after 'й' or before a soft consonant, such as the soft 'н' of 'ви́шня' and 'пі́сня' ('я́єць', 'ви́шень', 'пі́сень'). For other words, such as 'сестра́' and 'вікно́', learn the form with the word.

A stem that ends in a soft consonant keeps it soft at the end of the word, so the form is written with 'ь': 'неді́ля', 'неді́ль'; 'полуни́ця', 'полуни́ць'; 'ву́лиця', 'ву́лиць'. When an 'е' is inserted before 'н', the 'н' becomes hard and no 'ь' is written: 'ви́шня', 'ви́шень'; 'пі́сня', 'пі́сень'; and 'гри́вня', 'гри́вень', which you met after numbers.

In some words an 'о' of the stem becomes 'і', because it now stands in a closed syllable, by the rule you know from 'кіт', 'кота́':

- 'нога́', 'ніг'
- 'сло́во', 'слів'
- 'шко́ла', 'шкіл'

Not every 'о' changes ('мо́ва', 'мов'), so learn these with the word.

A small group takes '-ей':

- 'лю́ди', 'люде́й'
- 'ді́ти', 'діте́й'
- 'гро́ші', 'гроше́й'
- feminine nouns that end in a consonant, such as 'ніч', 'ноче́й'

Plural-only nouns and nouns used mostly in the plural follow the same patterns: 'штани́', 'штані́в'; 'кані́кули', 'кані́кул'; 'варе́ники', 'варе́ників'. The table gives each noun's nominative, singular wherever the noun has one, and its genitive plural.

rows: 'е' inserted; the stress moves to it

examples.source: There are no tomatoes in the shop.
These books are for students.
There are a lot of museums in Lviv.
I don't have any sisters.
I bought six cups.

grammar.title: Adjectives, possessives and the accusative plural
grammar.explanation:
In the plural an adjective has one set of endings for all three genders: 'нові́' goes with 'помідо́ри', 'пля́шки' and 'я́блука' alike, and the same holds in every case. The endings of an adjective with a hard stem are these:

- nominative '-і': 'нові́ кни́ги'
- genitive '-их': 'нови́х книг'
- dative '-им': 'нови́м студе́нтам'
- instrumental '-ими': 'з нови́ми дру́зями'
- locative '-их': 'у нови́х міста́х'

An adjective with a soft stem writes 'і' where a hard stem writes 'и': 'си́ні', 'си́ніх', 'си́нім', 'си́німи'. Possessive pronouns and the demonstratives 'цей' and 'той' take the same endings:

- 'мої́', 'мої́х', 'мої́м', 'мої́ми'
- 'на́ші', 'на́ших', 'на́шим', 'на́шими'
- 'ці', 'цих', 'цим', 'ци́ми'
- 'ті', 'тих', 'тим', 'ти́ми'

The words 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх' meaning his, her and their still never change: 'його́ дру́зі', 'з його́ дру́зями'.

The accusative plural has no ending of its own. Grammar calls nouns that name people or animals animate nouns. An animate noun uses its genitive form in the accusative; every other noun uses its nominative form. You learned this rule for masculine nouns in the singular ('Я ба́чу бра́та.'); in the plural it holds for all three genders:

- things: 'Я купу́ю помідо́ри.', 'Я купу́ю пля́шки.', 'Я купу́ю я́блука.'
- people: 'Я ба́чу студе́нтів.', 'Я ба́чу сесте́р.', 'Я ба́чу діте́й.'
- animals: 'Я ба́чу коті́в.'

An adjective or possessive takes the same form as its noun: 'Я купу́ю зеле́ні я́блука.', but 'Я запро́шую свої́х дру́зів.' The pronoun 'їх', them, is the accusative for people and for things alike: 'Помідо́ри? Я їх купи́в.'

examples.source: These green apples are very tasty.
I'm inviting my friends.

grammar.title: Numbers and words of quantity with nouns
grammar.explanation:
In the numbers unit you met 'два ро́ки' and 'п’ять ро́ків', 'дві гри́вні' and 'п’ять гри́вень' as forms to learn whole. Now that you know the plural cases, the rule behind them can be stated in full. The number decides the form of the noun:

- 'оди́н', 'одна́', 'одне́': the nominative singular, with the number agreeing in gender, as in 'оди́н кілогра́м', 'одна́ пля́шка', 'одне́ я́блуко'
- 'два' or 'дві', 'три', 'чоти́ри': the nominative plural, as in 'два кілогра́ми', 'три пля́шки', 'чоти́ри я́блука'
- 'п’ять' to 'де́сять', the numbers from eleven to nineteen, the round tens and 'сто': the genitive plural, as in 'п’ять кілогра́мів', 'одина́дцять пля́шок', 'сто я́блук'

The genitive after 'п’ять' has a history. The numbers from five up were once nouns meaning a group of five, a group of ten, and the things in a group follow in the genitive, as English says 'a group of friends' with 'of'. So 'п’ять ро́ків' is literally 'five of-years'.

In a compound number the last word decides: 'два́дцять одна́ гри́вня', 'два́дцять дві гри́вні', 'два́дцять п’ять гри́вень'. An adjective after 'два', 'три' and 'чоти́ри' is in the nominative plural, as in 'два нові́ студе́нти'; after 'п’ять' and higher numbers it is in the genitive plural, as in 'п’ять нови́х студе́нтів'.

Words of quantity take the genitive too:

- 'бага́то', a lot, many, much
- 'ма́ло', little, few
- 'кі́лька', several, a few
- 'до́сить', enough
- 'скі́льки', how much, how many

With a noun for something you count they take the genitive plural: 'бага́то люде́й', 'кі́лька я́блук'. With a noun for something you do not count, such as water, time or bread, they take the genitive singular: 'бага́то води́', 'ма́ло ча́су', 'до́сить хлі́ба'. 'Кі́лька' goes only with things you count.

Words for containers and measures are ordinary nouns, and what they hold follows in the genitive, where English uses 'of': 'пля́шка води́', 'паке́т молока́', 'шмато́к си́ру', 'кілогра́м помідо́рів', 'кілогра́м карто́плі'. Eggs are counted by the ten, 'деся́ток я́єць'. 'Пів', half, is written together with the noun after it, which is in the genitive singular: 'півкілогра́ма', 'півгоди́ни'. In telling the time it stays a separate word: 'пів на во́сьму'.

When a word of quantity is the subject, a verb in the past is neuter singular: 'На ри́нку було́ бага́то люде́й.' (There were a lot of people at the market, literally 'on market was many of-people.')

examples.source: I bought three kilograms of potatoes.
I have twenty-five hryvnias.
There weren't many people at the party.
A few plums, please.
We have enough time.

grammar.title: 'Люди́на' and 'лю́ди', 'дити́на' and 'ді́ти'
grammar.explanation:
'Люди́на' means a person or a human being, a man or a woman alike. It is a feminine noun, and that is a fact about the word, not about the person: an adjective or a pronoun with it is feminine whoever it names. 'Він ду́же ціка́ва люди́на.' means 'He is a very interesting person', with the feminine form 'ціка́ва'. 'Дити́на', child, works the same way for a boy or a girl.

The ordinary plurals of these two nouns are built on other stems: 'лю́ди', people, and 'ді́ти', children. They are the plurals of 'люди́на' and 'дити́на', not nouns of their own. In the plural they take the endings of this unit, except for two older endings:

- genitive and accusative '-ей': 'люде́й', 'діте́й'
- instrumental '-ьми': 'людьми́', 'дітьми́'

The dative and the locative take the soft endings: 'лю́дям', 'ді́тям' and 'на лю́дях', 'на ді́тях'.

After 'дві', 'три' and 'чоти́ри' these nouns do not use 'лю́ди' and 'ді́ти'. They use the plural of their own stem, 'люди́ни' and 'дити́ни': 'дві люди́ни', 'три дити́ни'. From 'п’ять' on, and after words of quantity, the form is the genitive plural 'люде́й' or 'діте́й': 'п’ять люде́й', 'бага́то діте́й'.

'Лю́ди' and 'ді́ти' take plural verbs and adjectives, like any plural noun: 'Ці лю́ди гово́рять украї́нською.'

examples.source: She is a nice person.
They have three children.

examples.target: Оле́на ча́сто гуля́є з дітьми́ в па́рку.
examples.source: Olena often goes for walks in the park with the children.
examples.source_literal: Olena often strolls with children in park.

examples.source: There are a lot of people in the metro.
These presents are for the children.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: пля́шок, сесте́р, я́єць and людьми́
grammar.explanation:
Every new word and form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The genitive plural brings up the points below.

An inserted vowel is a full vowel, said like any other. In 'пля́шок' [ˈplʲɑʃɔk] the stress stays on the stem, and the inserted 'о' keeps its full sound, since Ukrainian 'о' is never reduced. In 'сесте́р' [sɛsˈtɛr] the stress falls on the inserted 'е' itself, although 'сестра́' is stressed on the ending and 'се́стри' on the first syllable. 'Ві́кон' [ˈʋikɔn] has the stress on the stem, as 'ві́кна' does.

'Я́єць' [ˈjɑjɛt͡sʲ] comes from the stem 'яйц-' of 'яйце́'. An 'е' is inserted between 'й' and 'ц', and 'й' plus 'е' is written 'є', as at the start of a word. The word ends in a soft 'ць', as 'украї́нець' does.

In 'люде́й' [lʲuˈdɛj] the 'ю' softens the 'л', and the 'д' before 'е' is hard. In 'людьми́' [lʲudʲˈmɪ] and 'дітьми́' [dʲitʲˈmɪ] the soft sign makes the consonant before 'м' soft.

A masculine noun whose last 'о' or 'е' drops before an ending loses it before '-ів' too: 'ри́нок', 'ри́нків'; 'шмато́к', 'шматкі́в'; 'деся́ток', 'деся́тків'. In 'о́гірок' the stress also moves to the ending in the plural: 'огірки́', 'огіркі́в', 'огірка́ми'. 'Буря́к' does the same: 'буряки́', 'бурякі́в'.

The ending '-ів' ends in [w], as every 'в' does at the end of a syllable: 'помідо́рів', 'кілогра́мів'. Among the new words, 'я' softens the 'с' of 'деся́ток' and the 'н' of 'ви́шня', 'ю' softens the 'л' of 'люди́на', and the soft sign softens the 'л' of 'кі́лька' and the final 'т' of 'до́сить'.

'Сік', juice, has the genitive 'со́ку', which you need after 'пля́шка': the 'і' of the closed syllable is 'о' when the syllable opens, as in 'кіт', 'кота́'. The genitive plural 'ніг' of 'нога́' shows the same rule the other way: the syllable closes, and 'о' becomes 'і'.

I need fifteen eggs.

examples.source: How much is a kilogram of cucumbers?

culture.title: The market, the kilogram and the ten
culture.text:
'Ри́нок' is a market where farmers and small sellers offer fruit, vegetables, meat, milk, cheese and eggs, and every Ukrainian town has one. Many people prefer it to a supermarket for food that is fresh and in season. In Kyiv the best-known market is Bessarabskyi Market, in a covered hall in the city center that opened in 1912; most neighborhoods also have an open market with rows of stalls.

At a market, food is sold by weight, by the piece or by the ten:

- fruit, vegetables and potatoes by the kilogram: 'кілогра́м помідо́рів', 'півкілогра́ма ви́шень'
- cheese, meat and sausage by the piece, weighed after it is cut: 'шмато́к си́ру'
- eggs by the ten: 'деся́ток я́єць'
- milk in bottles or cartons: 'пля́шка молока́', 'паке́т молока́'

A buyer says 'Да́йте, будь ла́ска' and the amount, with the food that is measured in the genitive, and the seller often answers with a question: 'Скі́льки вам?', literally 'how-much to-you?', meaning 'How much would you like?'.

Each fruit has its season, and people look forward to it. Strawberries, 'полуни́ці', arrive at the end of May and fill the markets in June; sour cherries, 'ви́шні', follow in late June and July; plums and pears come in late summer. The sour cherry tree is a symbol of the Ukrainian home. In a well-known poem by Taras Shevchenko, the national poet, a small cherry orchard grows beside a village house. Varenyky filled with sour cherries, 'варе́ники з ви́шнями', are a favorite summer dish.

exercises.prompt: Match the fruit and vegetables with their English names
Match each amount with its English meaning

choices: There are a lot of people at the market today.
There are few children at the market today.
There are few people at the market today.

exercises.explanation: 'Бага́то' means a lot, and 'люде́й' is the genitive plural of 'лю́ди'. A few people is 'кі́лька люде́й', and two people is 'дві люди́ни'.

choices: We need six bottles of juice.
We need five bottles of juice.
We need six bottles of water.

exercises.prompt: Which endings does every noun take in the dative plural, whatever its gender?
exercises.explanation: The dative, instrumental and locative plural have the same endings for all genders: '-ам', '-ами' and '-ах' after a hard consonant, and '-ям', '-ями' and '-ях' after a soft consonant, a vowel or 'й'. '-ах' is the locative and '-ами' the instrumental.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'кни́га' is the genitive plural?
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns in '-а' take no ending in the genitive plural, so 'кни́га' becomes 'книг'. 'Кни́ги' is the nominative plural, and 'кни́гах' the locative plural.
After 'дві', 'три' and 'чоти́ри', 'дити́на' uses the plural of its own stem: 'три дити́ни'. 'Ді́ти' is the plural used without a number, and 'діте́й' follows 'п’ять' and higher numbers.

exercises.hint_source: How much is a kilogram of pears?
exercises.explanation: What is weighed follows 'кілогра́м' in the genitive. 'Гру́ша' takes no ending in the genitive plural: 'груш'.
After 'п’ять' the noun is in the genitive plural. Masculine nouns take '-ів', and 'о́гірок' loses its second 'о' and moves the stress to the ending: 'огіркі́в'.

exercises.hint_source: There are a lot of museums in our city.
exercises.explanation: After 'бага́то' a noun you count is in the genitive plural. After 'й' the ending '-ів' is written '-їв': 'музе́їв'.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana is giving the children apples.
exercises.explanation: The children receive the apples, so they are in the dative plural: 'ді́ти' takes '-ям', 'ді́тям'.

exercises.prompt_target: Я роблю́ сала́т із помідо́рами й ___.
exercises.hint_source: I'm making a salad with tomatoes and cucumbers.
exercises.explanation: 'Із' meaning with takes the instrumental, and the plural instrumental ending is '-ами': 'огірка́ми', with the stress on the ending as in every plural form of 'о́гірок'.
'Нема́є' takes the genitive. 'Гро́ші' is one of the few nouns with the genitive plural '-ей': 'гроше́й'.

exercises.hint_source: I bought strawberries for the children.
exercises.explanation: 'Для' takes the genitive, and the genitive plural of 'ді́ти' is 'діте́й', with the old ending '-ей'.

exercises.hint_source: I see my sisters at the market.
exercises.explanation: Sisters are people, so the accusative plural uses the genitive form, as 'свої́х' shows. 'Сестра́' takes no ending and inserts an 'е': 'сесте́р'.

exercises.hint_source: My friends live in new apartments.
exercises.explanation: 'У' meaning in takes the locative, and the locative plural of an adjective ends in '-их' for every gender: 'у нови́х кварти́рах'.

exercises.hint_source: There isn't much milk in the kitchen.
exercises.explanation: Milk is not counted, so after 'ма́ло' it is in the genitive singular: 'молока́'.

exercises.hint_source: A bottle of juice costs twenty-two hryvnias.
exercises.explanation: In a compound number the last word decides. It is 'дві', because 'гри́вня' is feminine, and after it the noun is in the nominative plural: 'два́дцять дві гри́вні'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'три пля́шки' but 'п’ять пля́шок'?
choices: 'Пля́шок' is the plural and 'пля́шки' the singular.
After 'два', 'три' and 'чоти́ри' the noun is in the nominative plural; after 'п’ять' and higher numbers it is in the genitive plural.
'Пля́шок' is used only for bottles of water.
exercises.explanation: 'Пля́шки' is the nominative plural and 'пля́шок' the genitive plural. The numbers from five up were once nouns, and the things counted follow them in the genitive.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'пля́шка' have the genitive plural 'пля́шок', with an 'о' that its other forms do not have?
choices: Without an ending the word would end in 'шк', so an 'о' is inserted between the two consonants.
'-ок' is the genitive plural ending of all feminine nouns.
The 'а' of 'пля́шка' becomes 'о' in every plural form.
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns in '-а' take no ending in the genitive plural. Ukrainian does not end this word in two consonants, so an 'о' appears between them, as in 'ча́шок' and 'ру́чок'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Я ба́чу дру́зів.' but 'Я купу́ю помідо́ри.'?
choices: 'Дру́зів' is the subject and 'помідо́ри' the object.
Only masculine nouns use the genitive form in the accusative.
Nouns that name people use the genitive form in the accusative plural; nouns that name things use the nominative form.
exercises.explanation: Friends are people, so the accusative plural is the genitive form 'дру́зів'. Tomatoes are things, so the accusative plural is the nominative form 'помідо́ри'. In the plural the rule holds for every gender: 'Я ба́чу сесте́р.'

exercises.prompt: Why is the adjective feminine in 'Він ду́же ціка́ва люди́на.'?
choices: 'Люди́на' is a feminine noun whoever it names, and the adjective agrees with the noun.
The sentence is about a woman.
exercises.explanation: 'Він' shows that the person is a man, but the adjective agrees with the noun 'люди́на', which is grammatically feminine. 'Дити́на' works the same way.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'бага́то люде́й' but 'бага́то води́'?
choices: After 'бага́то' a noun for something you count is in the genitive plural, and a noun for something you do not count is in the genitive singular.
'Бага́то' takes the genitive only with nouns for people.
exercises.explanation: People are counted, so 'бага́то' takes the genitive plural 'люде́й'. Water is not counted, so it takes the genitive singular 'води́', as 'ма́ло ча́су' and 'до́сить хлі́ба' do.

exercises.prompt: Which case is 'вихідни́х' in the phrase 'на вихідни́х'?
choices: The locative plural, with the adjective ending '-их'
exercises.explanation: 'На' here takes the locative, and 'вихідні́' declines like an adjective, so its locative plural ends in '-их'. Its nominative plural is 'вихідні́'.

exercises.prompt_source: There were a lot of people at the market.
I bought two kilograms of tomatoes.
How much are these sour cherries?
I need two bottles of water.
exercises.explanation: 'Тре́ба' takes the person in the dative. 'Пля́шка' is feminine, so the number is 'дві', and after it the noun is in the nominative plural; the water follows in the genitive.

exercises.prompt_source: We have a lot of friends.
exercises.explanation: 'Бага́то' takes the genitive plural of a noun you count: 'дру́зів'.
After 'п’ять', 'кілогра́м' is in the genitive plural, 'кілогра́мів'. Potatoes are not counted, so 'карто́пля' is in the genitive singular, 'карто́плі'.
Students are people, so the accusative plural uses the genitive form, for the adjective too: 'нови́х студе́нтів', or 'нови́х студе́нток' for women students.

exercises.hint_source: These tomatoes are red and tasty.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what does Bohdan not have today?
exercises.explanation: Bohdan says 'полуни́ць сього́дні нема́є', there are no strawberries today, with the genitive plural after 'нема́є'. Oksana takes half a kilogram of sour cherries instead.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, how many people will be at Olena's dinner, counting Olena and Taras?
exercises.explanation: The guests are their parents, their grandmother, their uncle and aunt and three children, and with Olena and Taras that makes 'де́сять люде́й'.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, whom did Sam buy the sour cherries for?
exercises.explanation: Sam answers 'Мої́м сусі́дам.', in the dative plural, because the neighbors are the people who receive the cherries.
